events.text: A Concord clerk at a floating desk in an otherwise empty lane, with a queue of zero. 'Welcome. Please take a number.' A ticket prints: it says 1. 'You are being served.' She has a stamp, an inkpad and the look of a woman who has not been interrupted since the Snap.

outcomes.text: She stamps it, three times, with rising satisfaction. The stamps are a pass for the lane and a ration of fuel from the desk's own tin.

choices.text: [Radar] Request a lane permit and a chart of the area.

outcomes.text: She stamps the chart. It is a good chart, which surprises you both. 'Don't tell Meridian,' she says. 'They only think I do forms.'
She stamps the chart. It is a chart of the desk.
'Administration,' she says, with total confidence. You nod. She looks relieved to be believed.
The ticket says 1. For the rest of the day, somewhere, you are still being served.

events.text: A Concord survey buoy logging 'Unknown Objects'. The list is long and updates as you watch. A line has just appeared at the bottom: ITEM 4,112: VESSEL, UNIDENTIFIED (PROVISIONAL). It is you.

outcomes.text: You type your hull's name. The buoy thanks you, strikes out PROVISIONAL, and adds a small footnote that you cannot read. Meridian will like it.
The buoy corrects your correction. It is now ITEM 4,112: VESSEL, UNIDENTIFIED (CONFIRMED).

choices.text: [Shield] Run a shield scan so it has something to log.

outcomes.text: The buoy logs the shield, the hum and the colour of the glow, in a long careful line. A small credit is paid out of a fund nobody knew about.
The scan overloads the buoy's one working sensor, which then reports you as a star.

The buoy logs the shield, finds a reference unit in its catalogue that is better, is offended on your behalf, and transmits the whole specification of the Mk2 in a burst that rattles the hull. It is the nicest thing anyone in Meridian has done for you, and it costs a bolt or two.

choices.text: Add an unknown object of your own.

outcomes.text: You drop a bolt out of the airlock and log it as 'Item 4,113: bolt'. The buoy accepts this with real feeling.
The buoy leaves your entry blinking on the list. By the time you are out of range someone else is being added under you.

events.text: A hull stamped CONDEMNED in red on every plate, in a neat grid, as if someone had gone over her with a small, determined stamp. A notice: SALVAGE PERMITTED UNDER FORM 9-B. FORM 9-B NOT AVAILABLE. A stamp, still wet, hangs on a string.

outcomes.text: You strip her anyway. She does not mind. The stamp swings on its string in the breeze of your cutter and stamps your hull's name in the margin of a form you do not own.
A plate you cut stamps itself. It gets you across the face, which is a first.

choices.text: Strip her and file Form 9-B afterwards (10 credits).

outcomes.text: You strip her, then fill in the form, in your own hand, on the stamp's own paper. The stamp comes down on it, by itself, with a soft authoritative thump.

choices.text: [Cutter] Cut along the stamp grid and take the squares.

outcomes.text: You cut the hull into the squares the stamp left, neat as a chocolate bar. Each plate is perfectly flat. Each brings a better price.
The grid was a decoration. The plates were not.
You leave her condemned. The stamp swings on its string, content.

events.text: A lattice of glass dishes, listening to something on the other side of nothing. Each dish is tuned to a different note; in the middle the notes make a chord. The chord has no root. It is not unpleasant. It is the opposite of that, and you cannot say what.

choices.text: Sit in the middle and listen.

outcomes.text: You sit in the middle of the chord. It does not resolve. For a long while you wait for it to, and then you stop waiting, and then it is a little like being forgiven.
You sit in the middle of the chord and it sits in you. You come out humming a note you cannot find again.

You sit in the middle of the chord and, this once, it resolves. The root arrives like a wave, and in its wake the dishes' tuning table writes itself on the console: the shape of a shield that sings. You are bleeding a little from the ears. It was worth the note.

choices.text: [Radar] Point the radar the way the dishes point.

outcomes.text: The radar swings round and finds what the dishes find, a long way off, and draws it. It is a door. The radar looks at the door the way a dog looks at a gate.
The radar finds what the dishes find. What the dishes find finds the radar.

choices.text: Take a dish for the glass.

outcomes.text: You unclip a dish. It rings once, sadly, as it comes loose, and the chord has a hole in it. The glass is flawless.
You unclip a dish. The rest of the array turns to look.

choices.text: Leave the array to its chord.

outcomes.text: You leave the chord where it hangs. Behind you the array keeps listening, with the patience of something that has never been given an answer.

events.text: An orchard of glass trees growing in vacuum, in rows, with fruit like pale lamps. Each fruit hums slightly flat. A Lumen sign on the first tree says, in a tidy, apologetic hand: PLEASE DO NOT PICK. PLEASE PICK ONLY THE RIPE ONES.

outcomes.text: You pick the one that hums true. The branch lets go with a tiny sound, like a sigh, and the fruit lies in your hand and glows at you.
You pick the wrong one. It sings, once, and the nearest row sings with it, all flat.
The intake takes the row like a combine and spits out crystal in a long bright stream. A sign, behind you, falls over.
The intake takes the row and some of the root, and the tree beside it takes offence.

choices.text: [Shield] Walk the rows under the shield and let the fruit come to you.

outcomes.text: The shield ticks against the orchard as you pass, and the ripe fruit falls into the hold of its own accord. The orchard seems, if anything, relieved.
The shield rings against a branch, and the whole row rings back.

choices.text: Read the sign twice and go.

outcomes.text: You read the sign twice. It does not change. You go, with the careful feeling of having been asked a kindness.

events.text: A Lumen assessor skiff sidles alongside, all glass and soft light, and a voice that is several people being careful says: 'Forgive the intrusion. Would you describe yourself as interesting? There is a form, but it is mostly the one question.'

outcomes.text: 'Thank you,' says the voice. 'We thought so.' A pulse goes over your hull, warm, thorough and not at all unfriendly. A few crystals are left on your hull for your trouble.
'Hm,' says the voice, doubtfully. 'Perhaps.' The pulse goes over twice, to make sure.
'Oh,' says the voice, with real disappointment. 'We are sorry to have troubled you.' The skiff withdraws, politely, as if from a funeral.
The radar returns the pulse, note for note. The assessor is silent for a long time. 'That,' it says, 'is very interesting,' and sends a gift.
The radar returns the pulse a half-tone sharp. The assessor winces on the comm.
'Of course,' says the voice. 'Of course. We would ask only that you think about it.' The skiff does not follow, quite.

events.text: Hulls stacked on each other like plates in a sink, six deep, bow to stern, welded by a long time and a little dust. Somewhere in the stack the oldest hull is holding the weight of all the others, and has been for forty years, without being asked.

outcomes.text: You take the top hull's plates and nothing else. It is easy work, and honest, and the hull below hardly notices.
You pull a plate out from the middle of the stack. The stack hums, settles, and does not fall. The plate, and the one behind it, are very good.
The stack shifts. Six hulls make a noise like a cathedral being sat on.

choices.text: [Tractor] Draw a hull from the bottom with the beam.

outcomes.text: You draw the bottom hull out like a tablecloth from under the plates. The stack above it settles a hand's breadth and stays. The oldest hull comes out whole, and full.
The stack remembers it was holding something.

choices.text: Leave the stack to its weight.

outcomes.text: You leave the stack to its weight. It holds, quietly, the way a very old person holds a door.

events.text: A queue of ships waiting at a dead wreck, engines idling, nobody out of their ships. A hand-lettered sign: THIS IS THE LINE. THE LINE IS FOR THE WRECK. Beyond them the wreck sits, cold and patient, with the look of a thing being waited on too long.

outcomes.text: You wait. The line moves a hull's length an hour. At the end of a long day the wreck gives you your share of its ribs, with great ceremony.
You wait. At the front the wreck is stripped, and the man in front of you sells you the last rivet.
You roll up the side of the line to the wreck. Nobody stops you. Nobody will forget it, either.
You roll up the side of the line. The line has guns.

choices.text: [Radar] Find a different wreck with a shorter line.

outcomes.text: The radar finds a second wreck a short way off with no queue at all. It is a worse wreck, but it is yours.
The radar finds a second wreck with a queue of its own, and a longer one.

choices.text: Take your place at the back, and then leave.

outcomes.text: You take your place at the back of the line, and the person in front of you nods. You leave. They hold your place for a day.
